sources.ref_file_title: GI14 - Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications
sources.note: EUROCRYPT 2014, pp. 640-658 (cryptobib EC:GilIsh14). 2-server computational PIR is the paper's flagship DPF application.

pages.class_justification: The construction calls the DPF only through $\Gen$ and $\Eval$ — one fixed construction with the hypothesis as an oracle. The privacy reduction is fixed and runs any query distinguisher once as an oracle: server $b$'s view is the single key $k_b$, so the distinguisher is verbatim an adversary against DPF key indistinguishability (GI14's security notion). RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: A [[distributed-point-function|DPF]] for domain $[N]$ and range $\ZZ_2$ yields a 2-server [[multi-server-private-information-retrieval#computational-multi-server-pir|computational PIR]] for an $N$-bit database $D$ in which each query is one DPF key and each answer one bit: the client sends $(k_0, k_1) \gets \Gen(1^\secpar, i, 1)$, one key to each server; server $b$ returns $a_b = \sum_{j \in [N]} D[j] \cdot \Eval(b, k_b, j)$; and $D[i] = a_0 + a_1$ — [[GI14 - Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications|GI14]].
pages.sketch: Correctness: $a_0 + a_1 = \sum_j D[j] \cdot f_{i,1}(j) = D[i]$ by DPF correctness. Privacy: server $b$'s entire view of a query is $k_b$, so a distinguisher between queries for $i$ and $i'$ is a DPF key-indistinguishability adversary with the same advantage.
notes_to_keep: The construction is inherently 2-server; the conclusion node computational-multi-server-pir does not record the server count.
flags: distributed-point-function.md § Hiding is a guess-the-point game with an ill-formed advantage ($\left|2\Pr[\calA(1^\secpar, k_b) = \alpha] - 1\right|$ is near $1$ for every $\calA$ once $N$ is large); GI14 define DPF security as key indistinguishability (a key for $(\alpha,\beta)$ vs one for $(\alpha',\beta')$), which is what this privacy reduction uses — fix the primitive page in the skeptical-checker lane.
The query length is the DPF key length; GI14's own DPF gives polylogarithmic queries only assuming a strong OWF (their abstract), so no parameter bound is recorded on this edge.

sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Geoffroy Couteau, Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
sources.note: ACM CCS 2018, pp. 896-912; cryptobib CCS:BCGI18 (verified in vendor/cryptobib); full version eprint 2019/273. Defines multi-point FSS (MPFSS) and constructs it from DPFs via combinatorial batch codes.

pages.class_justification: The combined $\Gen$ runs the DPF's $\Gen$ once per point and the combined $\Eval$ sums the component calls — one fixed construction using the DPF only as an oracle. The proof is a fixed hybrid over the $t$ instances that runs any distinguisher as an oracle. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: A multi-point function with value $\beta_i$ at each of $t$ distinct points $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_t$ is the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{t} f_{\alpha_i, \beta_i}$ of point functions; sharing each summand with an independent [[distributed-point-function|DPF]] and summing the component shares in $\Eval$ gives a [[distributed-point-function#multi-point-functions|multi-point FSS]] whose keys are $t$ DPF keys — folklore.
pages.sketch: Correctness is additivity of the shares. Hiding is a hybrid over the $t$ instances, swapping one key at a time, so any distinguisher yields a DPF key-indistinguishability adversary with a factor-$t$ loss.
pages.security_loss: factor $t$ over the DPF key-indistinguishability advantage (hybrid over the $t$ instances)
pages.improvements_text: - Multi-point FSS (MPFSS) defined explicitly and built from DPFs via combinatorial batch codes, so that full-domain evaluation costs linear in $N$ rather than the naive construction's $t$ full DPF evaluations — [[BCGI18 - Compressing Vector OLE|BCGI18]]

sources.ref_file_title: Rom90 - One-way functions are necessary and sufficient for secure signatures
sources.note: STOC 1990, pp. 387-394; cryptobib STOC:Rompel90 (verified in vendor/cryptobib; DOI matches). The paper's main content is sufficiency (OWF ⇒ DS via UOWHFs); the necessity direction recorded by this edge is the easy one asserted by the title, and the literature cites this paper for the equivalence.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction — $f$ runs $\KeyGen$ on its input coins and outputs the verification key — using the scheme only as an oracle, and one fixed reduction that runs any inverter once as an oracle and signs under the recovered key. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: If a perfectly correct EUF-CMA-secure [[digital-signature|DS]] scheme exists then so does a one-way function ([[hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness|OWF]]): $f(r) := \vk$, where $(\sk, \vk) := \KeyGen(1^\secpar; r)$, is one-way, since an inverter returns coins $r'$ whose signing key $\sk'$ produces signatures valid under $\vk$ on every message — a forgery with no signing query — [[Rom90 - One-way functions are necessary and sufficient for secure signatures|Rom90]].
pages.sketch: An inverter for $f$ returns $r'$ with $\KeyGen(1^\secpar; r') = (\sk', \vk)$; perfect correctness makes $\Sign(\sk', m)$ verify under $\vk$ for every $m$, so the inverter's success probability lower-bounds the forger's, which unforgeability makes negligible.
flags: The origin bullet on digital-signature.md justifies the claim with a secrecy statement ('knowing the message and signature reveals nothing useful about the key'), which is not the argument — that page's prose needs the same fix (skeptical-checker lane; matches this page's migration SUSPECTED note).

'Perfectly correct' is load-bearing: digital-signature.md defines only $(1-\varepsilon)$-correctness over $\KeyGen$'s coins, under which an inverter may return coins whose signing key fails to sign; the argument needs every key pair in $\KeyGen$'s support to sign correctly (or a separate treatment of bad coins).

Conclusion node hash-function conflates OWF with CRHF: the statement is scoped to OWF (anchored link). DS does NOT imply collision-resistant hashing — black-box separation by Simon, Eurocrypt 1998 (cryptobib EC:Simon98) — do not let the coarse node suggest otherwise.
Converse direction OWF ⇒ DS exists as its own page (hash-function-to-ds.md), for which Rom90 is also the canonical source — kind stays implication on both.

sources.ref_file_title: EGL85 - A randomized protocol for signing contracts
sources.authors: Shimon Even, Oded Goldreich, Abraham Lempel
sources.note: CACM 28(6):637-647, June 1985. Preliminary version CRYPTO 1982, pp. 205-210 — cryptobib C:EveGolLem82, DOI 10.1007/978-1-4757-0602-4_19 (verified in vendor/cryptobib; cryptobib has no entry for the CACM version, so its DOI is from memory and should be confirmed by the reference-fixer). Introduces 1-out-of-2 OT and the trapdoor-permutation protocol.

sources.ref_file_title: Gol04 - Foundations of Cryptography Basic Applications
sources.venue: Cambridge University Press, 2004 (Foundations of Cryptography, Volume 2)
sources.note: Book; cryptobib Goldreich04 (verified in vendor/cryptobib). Defines enhanced trapdoor permutations (Appendix C.1) and proves the EGL protocol secure for semi-honest parties under that hypothesis (Chapter 7); GR13's abstract credits the notion to this book.
Pins down which enhancements the EGL OT protocol needs (enhanced TDPs) versus NIZK (doubly enhanced).

pages.class_justification: The protocol uses the TDP only through $\Gen$, $\Eval$, $\Invert$ and the domain sampler, plus a Goldreich–Levin predicate — one fixed construction with the hypothesis as an oracle. Receiver privacy is statistical. The sender-privacy reduction is fixed and uses any receiver-view distinguisher only as an oracle, turning it via the black-box Goldreich–Levin decoder into an inverter of the enhanced TDP. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: An [[trapdoor-permutation#enhanced-trapdoor-permutations|enhanced trapdoor permutation]] yields 1-out-of-2 [[oblivious-transfer|OT]] secure against semi-honest parties, via the EGL protocol: the sender samples $(f, \td) \gets \Gen(1^\secpar)$ and sends $f$; the receiver with choice bit $c$ picks $x_c$ uniformly, samples $y_{1-c}$ obliviously from the domain, and sends $(y_0, y_1)$ with $y_c = \Eval(f, x_c)$; the sender returns $m_b \oplus h(\Invert(\td, y_b))$ for $b \in \bits$, where $h$ is a hard-core predicate — [[EGL85 - A randomized protocol for signing contracts|EGL85]]. Enhanced one-wayness — $f$ stays hard to invert on an obliviously sampled $y$ even given the sampling coins — is what keeps $m_{1-c}$ hidden from the receiver, who holds those coins — [[Gol04 - Foundations of Cryptography Basic Applications|Gol04]].
pages.sketch: Receiver privacy: $(y_0, y_1)$ are two independent uniform domain elements (up to the sampler's statistical error) whatever $c$ is. Sender privacy: a receiver that predicts $h(f^{-1}(y_{1-c}))$ from $y_{1-c}$'s sampling coins predicts a hard-core bit of an obliviously sampled image, and the Goldreich–Levin decoder turns it into an inverter contradicting enhanced one-wayness.
pages.improvements_text:
- Introduces the enhanced one-wayness hypothesis under which the EGL protocol is proven secure; for a TDP whose domain sampler's coins reveal a preimage the protocol is insecure — [[Gol04 - Foundations of Cryptography Basic Applications|Gol04]]
- Systematic treatment of the enhancement axis: enhanced TDPs suffice for EGL oblivious transfer, while NIZK needs doubly enhanced TDPs; intermediate notions separated — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]]
flags: SOURCE REPLACED: GKM+00 (FOCS 2000) is the PKE-vs-OT black-box separation paper; it predates the term 'enhanced TDP' (Goldreich 2004, per GR13's abstract) and only cites the EGL construction as background. Sources are now EGL85 (protocol), Gol04 (enhanced hypothesis and proof), GR13. The slug suffix -gkm-00 is therefore misleading, but filenames are live URLs — leave the rename decision to a human (precedent: red-01, red-03).
Statement scoped to semi-honest security; malicious security follows via the GMW compiler — standard.

The variant blurb on trapdoor-permutation.md misstates the enhancement ('a random element $y = \Eval(f, x)$ sampled using $r$'): $y$ is sampled directly from the domain with coins $r$, and hardness is inverting $y$ given $r$; fix on the primitive page.

sources.ref_file_title: Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions
sources.note: EUROCRYPT 2022 Part II, pp. 217-241; cryptobib EC:Wee22 (verified in vendor/cryptobib). The CP-ABE theorem assumes evasive LWE AND tensor LWE (both introduced there), plus LWE; the key queries and challenge policy are fixed in advance in the security model.

pages.model_justification: Standard-model construction; evasive LWE and tensor LWE are (non-standard) assumptions, not idealized models.
pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#evasive-lwe|Evasive LWE]], together with the tensor LWE assumption introduced in the same work (and [[learning-with-errors|LWE]]), yields ciphertext-policy [[attribute-based-encryption|ABE]] for circuits of a-priori bounded polynomial depth with parameter sizes independent of the circuit size; security is proven for adversaries that fix the challenge policy and their key queries in advance (very selective) — [[Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions|Wee22]].

sources.ref_file_title: Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions

pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#evasive-lwe|Evasive LWE]] (with [[learning-with-errors|LWE]]) yields optimal [[broadcast-encryption|BE]]: for $N$ users, the public key, each secret key, and the ciphertext are all of size $\poly(\secpar, \log N)$, with security proven selectively (the adversary fixes the recipient set before seeing the public key). It is the first optimal-BE candidate that is plausibly post-quantum secure — [[Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions|Wee22]].

pages.wrong_reason: Inverted, as both the page's own SUSPECTED notes and .reductions/suspected-errors.json record. Given the factorization of $n$ one computes $\varphi(n)$ and decides $n$-th residuosity in $\ZZ_{n^2}^*$ by testing $z^{\varphi(n)} \bmod n^2$, so a factoring algorithm breaks DCR; hence DCR hardness implies factoring hardness — DCR is the stronger assumption. The converse (factoring hard ⇒ DCR hard) is open, and Pai99 proves no such implication (Pai99 only notes the scheme falls to factoring). Correct edge: DCR ⇒ FAC (folklore; a dcr-to-fac page does not yet exist in content/Reductions/).

sources.ref_file_title: GMR88 - A Digital Signature Scheme Secure Against Adaptive Chosen-Message Attacks
sources.authors: Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, Ronald L. Rivest
sources.note: SIAM J. Comput. 17(2):281-308 (cryptobib GolMicRiv88). Defines EUF-CMA and constructs the first scheme meeting it, generically from claw-free trapdoor permutation pairs, with a factoring-based instantiation.

pages.class_justification: One fixed (stateful, tree-based) construction generic over claw-free trapdoor permutation pairs, used only as oracles; one fixed security reduction that runs any forger as an oracle and converts its forgery into a claw, which for the factoring-based pair yields the factorization of the challenge modulus. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: If [[factoring|FAC]] is hard then an EUF-CMA-secure [[digital-signature|DS]] scheme exists: GMR build a stateful signature scheme, secure against existential forgery under adaptive chosen-message attack, from any claw-free pair of trapdoor permutations, and instantiate claw-free pairs from factoring — [[GMR88 - A Digital Signature Scheme Secure Against Adaptive Chosen-Message Attacks|GMR88]].
pages.sketch: Signing authenticates the message and the path to a fresh leaf of an authentication tree with inverses of the claw-free pair $(f_0, f_1)$; the reduction turns any forgery into a claw $(x_0, x_1)$ with $f_0(x_0) = f_1(x_1)$, which for the factoring-based pair (squaring modulo $N$) reveals a nontrivial square root of $1$ modulo $N$, hence the factorization of $N$.
flags: The migration note is right that 'based on factoring' hides the intermediate object: the generic hypothesis is a claw-free trapdoor permutation pair; the statement now names it. If the wiki ever adds a claw-free-permutation node, split this edge into FAC ⇒ claw-free pair ⇒ DS.
The origin bullet on digital-signature.md lacks a wikilink to factoring — fix when applying.

pages.wrong_reason: Inverted, as the page's own SUSPECTED notes and .reductions/suspected-errors.json record (high confidence there too). Knowing $p$ and $q$ lets one compute Legendre symbols mod $p$ and $q$ and thereby decide quadratic residuosity mod $N = pq$, so a factoring algorithm breaks QR; hence QR hardness implies factoring hardness — QR is the stronger assumption. Whether factoring hardness implies QR hardness is a long-standing open question, and GM84 makes no such claim (GM84 introduce the QR assumption and prove semantic security of their scheme under it). The bullet's own justification ('knowing $p$ and $q$ allows computing the Legendre symbols') proves the opposite direction of the one asserted. Correct edge: QR ⇒ FAC (folklore; a qr-to-fac page does not yet exist in content/Reductions/).
